title: The motor unit: horn cell, nerve, junction, muscle
description: The four parts of the motor unit where weakness can begin, from the anterior horn cell to the muscle, and the pattern each one leaves on the examination.
why: Weakness in the motor unit can arise in four places, and each leaves its own pattern of distribution, reflexes, sensation, fatigue and fasciculations, so you can name the address before the EMG.
objectives: Separate anterior horn, nerve, junction and muscle disease using distribution, reflexes, sensation, fatigability and fasciculations.
Recognize the proximal pattern of myopathy and the Gowers maneuver in a young child.
Recognize fatigable ocular and bulbar weakness, and the presentation of infant botulism.
Explain why polyneuropathy is length-dependent, and what a pattern that breaks the rule suggests.
Recognize the purely motor, areflexic, fasciculating picture of anterior horn disease in an infant and a child.

sections.title: Telling the four addresses of the motor unit apart
sections.content:
Once the first fork has pointed to the motor unit, it is tempting to write "neuromuscular" in the notes and hand the child over to the electromyographer, and it is a temptation worth resisting. The motor unit is the anterior horn cell together with its axon and every muscle fiber that the axon supplies. Within it there are four addresses, which are the **cell body** in the anterior horn, the **axon** in the nerve, the **junction** where the axon meets the muscle, and the **muscle** itself. Each fails in a way that leaves its own fingerprint, and the fingerprints can be read at the bedside. A lower motor neuron lesion can lie anywhere from the motor neuron through the roots, plexus and nerves to the junction and the muscle (Brazis 2011, p. 12). [[m05-roots-plexus-nerves|Module 5]] covers the roots and plexus, and this module works through the other four sites.

**The fingerprint table**

| Feature | Horn cell | Nerve | Junction | Muscle |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Distribution | Proximal or patchy, often asymmetric | Distal and length-dependent, or one nerve's territory | Ocular, bulbar, proximal | Proximal and symmetric |
| Reflexes | Lost early | Lost early | Usually kept | Kept until the muscle is too weak to contract |
| Sensation | Normal | Often lost | Normal | Normal |
| Fatigue | No | No | Worse with use, better with rest | No |
| Fasciculations, wasting | Yes | With chronic axon loss | No | No |

Read the table down each column first, and then across the rows. Two of the rows do most of the sorting. **Sensation** separates the nerve from the other three addresses, because the horn cell, the junction and the muscle are purely motor. **Reflexes** separate the horn cell and the nerve, which lose them early, from the junction and the muscle, which keep them until late.

**Using the figure**

The figure above is the localizer loaded with motor-unit findings, along with three cases to try. For the boy who climbs up his legs, horn cell and muscle stay tied. That tie is the honest answer, because it tells you that the next finding to look for is a fasciculating tongue. The child with high arches and numb toes leaves only the nerve standing, and the teenager whose lids droop by evening leaves the junction on top.

**What changes in a child**

In an infant most of these signs are harder to elicit, and the presenting complaint is often hypotonia rather than weakness. The same four addresses still apply, and [[m03-first-fork|Module 3]] shows how to decide first whether a floppy infant's problem is central at all. At any age it pays to commit to an address before the electrodiagnostic study, because the test is far more useful when it has been asked a specific question.
keyPoints: The motor unit has four addresses, which are the anterior horn cell, the nerve, the neuromuscular junction and the muscle.
Sensory loss points to the nerve, because the horn cell, junction and muscle are purely motor.
Early loss of reflexes points to the horn cell or nerve, while the junction and muscle keep reflexes until late.
Fatigability is the signature of the junction, and fasciculations with wasting point to the horn cell or to chronic axon loss.
Committing to an address before the EMG means the test is answering a question.

question.question: A 6-year-old has weak hips and shoulders on both sides. Sensation is normal, reflexes are present though reduced, there are no fasciculations, and the weakness does not fatigue. Which address fits best?
options: Peripheral nerve, because the reflexes are reduced
Neuromuscular junction, because the weakness is proximal
Muscle, because the weakness is proximal, symmetric and purely motor with reflexes still present
Anterior horn cell, because the weakness is purely motor
question.explanation: Proximal, symmetric, purely motor weakness with reflexes that are reduced but still present is the fingerprint of muscle disease, because in a myopathy the reflexes fade in proportion to the weakness instead of disappearing early. A neuropathy would usually bring sensory loss and a distal, length-dependent pattern, and reduced reflexes on their own do not outweigh those absences. The junction can weaken proximal muscles, but its defining feature, fatigability, is missing here. Anterior horn disease is purely motor as well, yet it tends to remove reflexes early and to cause fasciculations and wasting, and this child has none of them.

sections.title: Muscle: the girdles fail first
sections.content:
Muscle disease tends to show itself first in the muscles that hold the hips and shoulders against gravity. In most myopathies these girdle muscles fail first, so the typical result is **proximal, symmetric weakness** without sensory loss. This is the child who cannot get up off the floor, climb the stairs or lift a heavy book onto a high shelf, but whose hands and feet still work well.

The classic example is a boy with Duchenne muscular dystrophy (Brazis 2011, p. 13). He has **enlarged calves**, and to stand he uses the **Gowers maneuver**, pushing up on his own thighs because his hip extensors are weak. He also has an exaggerated lumbar curve, a waddling, wide-based gait, and a habit of walking on his toes. Most of these signs follow from proximal weakness. The waddle comes from weak hip abductors that cannot hold the pelvis level. The lumbar curve comes from leaning the trunk back to keep the center of gravity behind the weak hips.

**Muscle disease does not respect maps**

Roots and nerves supply muscles in fixed groups, so a root or nerve lesion weakens a predictable set of them, whereas muscle disease ignores those maps. In a dystrophy one muscle can be wasted while its neighbor, which shares the same root, is spared, and the same selective pattern appears in spinal muscular atrophy (Morris 2012, p. 17). When a pattern of weakness makes no sense in terms of roots or nerves, the muscle and the horn cell are the addresses to consider.

**Reflexes and sensation**

Sensation stays normal in muscle disease. The reflexes are kept until the muscle can no longer contract well enough to produce one. A child who has lost the reflexes while the muscles are still fairly strong therefore points away from the muscle and toward the horn cell or nerve.

**At the bedside**

Before any formal testing, watch the child rise from the floor. It is the most efficient test of hip strength there is, and a child will happily do it as part of a game. Look at the calves, at the shoulder blades for winging, and at the face. Keep in mind that the Gowers maneuver tells you the hips are weak without naming a disease, since spinal muscular atrophy and inflammatory myopathy produce it as well. The individual diseases are covered in detail in the site's [Neuromuscular](/neuromuscular) section.
keyPoints: Myopathy usually causes proximal, symmetric weakness that is purely motor.
Boys with Duchenne dystrophy show enlarged calves, a Gowers maneuver, lumbar lordosis, a waddling gait and toe walking (Brazis 2011, p. 13).
A Gowers maneuver shows weak hip extensors and does not identify a specific disease.
Selective wasting that ignores root and nerve maps suggests disease of the muscle or the horn cell (Morris 2012, p. 17).
Reflexes persist in myopathy until the muscle is very weak.

question.question: A 4-year-old boy pushes up on his thighs to stand from the floor. Taken on its own, what does that sign establish?
options: Weakness of the hip extensors, without saying which part of the motor unit is at fault
Duchenne muscular dystrophy
An upper motor neuron lesion in the spinal cord
A length-dependent peripheral neuropathy
question.explanation: The Gowers maneuver is a way of standing up when the hip extensors are too weak to lift the trunk, so on its own it establishes proximal leg weakness and nothing more specific. Duchenne dystrophy is the classic cause, but spinal muscular atrophy and the inflammatory myopathies produce the same maneuver, which makes naming Duchenne from this sign alone premature. A cord lesion gives spastic legs with brisk reflexes and no girdle pattern. A length-dependent neuropathy weakens the feet first, so the child would struggle to walk on his heels long before he had trouble getting up from the floor.

sections.title: The junction: weakness that wears out
sections.content:
Most weakness holds still for the examiner, in the sense that a weak muscle is weak whenever you test it. Weakness at the neuromuscular junction behaves differently, and recognizing that difference is most of the diagnosis. Each nerve impulse normally releases more than enough transmitter to fire the muscle fiber, so transmission has a safety margin. That margin can shrink because of antibodies against the acetylcholine receptor, a toxin that blocks release, or an inherited fault in the synapse. When it does, the first few impulses still succeed while later ones fail. The result is **weakness that worsens with use and recovers with rest**.

The hallmark of myasthenia gravis is fluctuating weakness with a predilection for the eye muscles and the proximal limbs, worse with exercise and better with rest (Brazis 2011, p. 13). The muscles of the eyes and eyelids are the most often involved, followed by those of chewing, swallowing and speech. The commonest first complaints are therefore **drooping lids and double vision that come and go**, while the reflexes are usually kept and sensation is normal.

**Testing fatigue**

The aim is to make the weakness happen in front of you. Ask for sustained upgaze and watch the lids fall, or ask the child to count aloud and listen as the voice fades. Testing a shoulder again and again will show whether the tenth effort is weaker than the first. A child who keeps up with friends at the start of a game but falls behind by the end is describing the same thing.

> **Bedside trick.** Lift one drooping lid with a finger, hold it there, and watch the other lid. In myasthenia it may sink further, a sign called enhanced ptosis. Then ask the child to squeeze the eyes shut and hold them closed. As the orbicularis tires, the lids part and the child seems to peek (Brazis 2011, p. 181). Enhanced ptosis is not specific to myasthenia, so it counts as supporting evidence rather than proof (Brazis 2011, p. 181).

**The junction in an infant**

Three disorders of the junction matter most in children. **Juvenile myasthenia gravis** behaves much like the adult disease. **Congenital myasthenic syndromes** are inherited faults of the synapse that are present from early life. **Infant botulism** is acquired, and in it a toxin blocks the release of transmitter. Suspect it in an infant under 6 months with acute or subacute floppiness together with constipation, listlessness, poor feeding, a weak cry and a reduced gag ([Peredo 2009](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19726697/)). The constipation is the clue that an autonomic, cholinergic synapse is failing too. When a floppy infant has ptosis, a weak suck and new constipation, the junction is the first address to consider.
keyPoints: Weakness at the junction worsens with use and recovers with rest, because the safety margin of transmission is reduced.
Myasthenia favors the eye muscles and proximal limbs (Brazis 2011, p. 13), and reflexes and sensation are usually normal.
Fatigue can be provoked at the bedside with sustained upgaze, counting aloud or repeated testing of one muscle.
Infant botulism should be suspected under 6 months when floppiness comes with constipation, poor feeding, a weak cry and a reduced gag (Peredo 2009).

question.question: A 3-month-old has been constipated for several days and is now floppy, with a weak suck, a weak cry and drooping eyelids. Which address fits all of the findings?
options: Anterior horn cell, as in spinal muscular atrophy
Peripheral nerve, as in Guillain-Barré syndrome
Muscle, as in a congenital myopathy
Neuromuscular junction, as in infant botulism
question.explanation: Ptosis, a weak suck and a weak cry reflect ocular and bulbar weakness, in the muscles the junction favors, and constipation shows that a cholinergic autonomic synapse is failing too. This cluster in an infant under 6 months is the reason to suspect infant botulism (Peredo 2009). Spinal muscular atrophy weakens the limbs and bulbar muscles but spares the eye muscles and does not cause constipation. Guillain-Barré syndrome is rare at this age and would bring areflexic limb weakness first. A congenital myopathy is present from birth and does not explain constipation that is new.

sections.title: Nerve: the longest axons fail first
sections.content:
A nerve cell body has to supply its entire axon with everything it needs, and the longest axons in the body are the ones that run to the feet. When a neuron is poisoned, starved or genetically weakened, it cannot keep the far end of a long axon going, and the axon dies back from its tip. In this dying-back process the largest neurons with the longest axons are affected first (Brazis 2011, p. 5). That one idea accounts for the shape of most polyneuropathies.

**Length dependence**

Symptoms therefore begin in the toes and climb from there. In a motor neuropathy the small foot muscles usually fail first, then the muscles supplied by the peroneal nerve, and then the calf. The intrinsic hand muscles become involved once everything below the knee is affected (Brazis 2011, p. 26). In the same way, symptoms in the hands are not usually seen until the legs are affected up to the knees (Pearl 2014, p. 76). The result is the **glove-and-stocking** pattern of sensory loss, and the ankle reflexes are lost first because their reflex arc is the longest.

**A rule that warns you off**

Because the nerve to the anterior compartment is longer, a neuropathy weakens dorsiflexion before plantar flexion. A patient who can walk on the heels but not on the toes therefore probably has an intraspinal problem, such as spinal muscular atrophy or a conus or cauda equina lesion, rather than a polyneuropathy (Brazis 2011, p. 26).

**Neuropathy in children**

In a child, a slowly progressive, symmetric neuropathy that has been present since early life suggests an inherited cause. The most familiar is **Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease**, with its high arches, thin lower legs, absent ankle reflexes and steppage gait. Early wasting of the first dorsal interosseous in the hand and of the short toe extensor on the foot has localizing value for a neuropathy (Brazis 2011, p. 11). An acute, ascending, areflexic weakness that develops over days is **Guillain-Barré syndrome**. It damages the roots as well as the nerves, so the localizer is right to keep both alive.
keyPoints: The longest axons fail first because they die back from the tip, so polyneuropathy starts in the feet (Brazis 2011, p. 5).
The hands become involved once the legs are affected to about the knees (Pearl 2014, p. 76; Brazis 2011, p. 26).
Ankle reflexes are lost first, and sensory loss takes a glove-and-stocking shape.
A patient who can walk on the heels but not the toes more likely has an intraspinal cause than a polyneuropathy (Brazis 2011, p. 26).
In a child, a lifelong symmetric neuropathy suggests an inherited cause, and an acute ascending one suggests Guillain-Barré syndrome.

question.question: A 10-year-old with slowly worsening leg weakness can walk on her heels but cannot walk on her toes. Ankle reflexes are absent and sensation is normal. What does the heel-toe pattern argue against?
options: A spinal muscular atrophy
A length-dependent polyneuropathy, which weakens dorsiflexion before plantar flexion
A conus or cauda equina lesion
An anterior horn cell disorder of any cause
question.explanation: In a length-dependent neuropathy the longer nerve to the anterior compartment fails before the nerve to the calf, so heel walking is lost before toe walking. The reverse pattern, with normal sensation, makes a polyneuropathy unlikely and points toward an intraspinal cause (Brazis 2011, p. 26). Spinal muscular atrophy and other anterior horn disorders are among those intraspinal causes, so the pattern suggests them instead of arguing against them. The same is true of a conus or cauda equina lesion.

sections.title: The anterior horn: weakness without numbness
sections.content:
The anterior horn cell lives inside the spinal cord, yet a child whose anterior horn cells are dying looks weak, floppy and areflexic, just like a patient with peripheral disease. That apparent contradiction shows what localization really means. We localize to the **function that is lost**, and here the lost function is the lower motor neuron, which happens to be housed in the cord.

**The fingerprint**

Anterior horn disease combines weakness with **wasting and fasciculations**, lost reflexes and **no sensory loss at all**. Fasciculations are visible twitches of small groups of muscle fibers, and they may accompany lower motor neuron disease (Brazis 2011, p. 11). They arise when sick motor units fire on their own. In a weak infant, look at the **tongue at rest inside the mouth**, where fine, writhing fasciculations are the classic sign of spinal muscular atrophy. The tongue has to be watched at rest, because a protruded tongue often quivers in healthy children too.

**Two very different stories**

**Spinal muscular atrophy** is a genetic loss of anterior horn cells. The infant is alert, socially bright and floppy, with a bell-shaped chest from weak intercostal muscles, absent reflexes and tongue fasciculations. Early recognition matters because disease-modifying treatments now exist, and the site's [Neuromuscular](/neuromuscular) section covers them.

**Acute flaccid myelitis** is an acquired injury to the gray matter of the cord, often after a viral illness. The weakness comes on over hours to days and is often asymmetric. It may involve a single limb, with absent reflexes in the weak limb and little or no sensory loss. This is a lower motor neuron fingerprint with its address in the cord, which is why the work-up is an MRI of the spine, as [[m06-spinal-cord|Module 6]] explains.

**Caveats**

Brief, isolated fasciculations in a healthy person are common and usually harmless. Fasciculations also appear with chronic damage to a root or nerve, which is why the localizer keeps root and nerve alive when you select fasciculations. What clinches the horn cell is finding fasciculations, wasting, areflexia and normal sensation together in the same child.
keyPoints: Anterior horn disease causes weakness, wasting, fasciculations and lost reflexes with normal sensation.
Look for tongue fasciculations with the tongue at rest inside the mouth, because a protruded tongue often quivers in healthy children too.
Spinal muscular atrophy presents as an alert, floppy, areflexic infant with tongue fasciculations, and early recognition matters because treatments exist.
Acute flaccid myelitis causes acute, often asymmetric, areflexic weakness from injury to the gray matter of the cord.
Brief, isolated fasciculations in a healthy person are common and usually harmless.

question.question: A 5-year-old develops floppy weakness of one arm over two days after a cold. The arm's reflexes are absent and sensation is normal; bladder function is normal. Which address best explains the picture?
options: Brachial plexus, as in neuralgic amyotrophy
A single peripheral nerve
Anterior horn cells of the cervical cord, as in acute flaccid myelitis
Muscle, as in viral myositis
question.explanation: Acute, asymmetric, flaccid and areflexic weakness of one limb with normal sensation is the lower motor neuron fingerprint of anterior horn injury, and after a viral illness acute flaccid myelitis is the diagnosis to exclude with an MRI of the spine. A brachial plexus lesion affects both motor and sensory fibers and is usually painful, so normal sensation argues against it. A single peripheral nerve cannot weaken a whole limb. Viral myositis causes muscle pain and tenderness, often in both calves, and keeps the reflexes, so it does not produce an areflexic paralysis of one limb.

quiz.question: A 14-year-old's eyelids droop by the end of the school day and she sees double after reading. Pupils are normal and reflexes are brisk-normal. At the bedside, which test best supports your localization?
options: A pinprick examination of the face
Sustained upgaze for a minute, watching whether the lids progressively fall
A strong flash of light to look for a sluggish pupil
Tapping the jaw to look for a brisk jaw jerk
quiz.explanation: Ptosis and diplopia that fluctuate and worsen through the day point to the neuromuscular junction, and the best bedside support is to provoke the fatigue with sustained upgaze and watch the lids fall progressively. Pinprick testing examines sensation, which the junction does not affect. A sluggish pupil would suggest a compressive lesion of the third nerve, and because myasthenia spares the pupil, the flash test cannot confirm the junction. A brisk jaw jerk is an upper motor neuron sign above the pons and says nothing about fatigable weakness.

quiz.question: A 4-month-old lies in a frog-leg posture, follows faces and smiles, has no reflexes and has fine writhing movements of the tongue at rest. Which address is most likely?
options: Cerebral hemispheres, as in central hypotonia
Neuromuscular junction
Muscle, as in congenital myopathy
Anterior horn cell, as in spinal muscular atrophy
quiz.explanation: An alert, socially engaged, floppy infant with absent reflexes and tongue fasciculations is the classic picture of spinal muscular atrophy, a loss of anterior horn cells. Central hypotonia usually comes with a depressed level of consciousness and normal or brisk reflexes (Peredo 2009), the opposite of this infant. Junction disorders spare the reflexes and do not cause fasciculations. A congenital myopathy keeps its reflexes longer and never fasciculates, because fasciculations come from a diseased motor neuron or its axon.

quiz.question: An 8-year-old has high arches, thin calves, absent ankle reflexes, a slapping gait and reduced vibration sense at the toes. Which address fits?
options: Peripheral nerve, a length-dependent neuropathy
Muscle, a distal myopathy
Anterior horn cell
A single lumbar root
quiz.explanation: Distal weakness with lost ankle reflexes and reduced vibration sense at the toes follows a length-dependent pattern, in which the longest axons have failed first, and of the four addresses only the nerve carries both motor and sensory fibers. Lifelong high arches and thin calves suggest an inherited neuropathy such as Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease. A distal myopathy would not cause sensory loss, and the anterior horn is purely motor. A single lumbar root would give a one-sided, dermatomal pattern instead of a symmetric distal one.

quiz.question: A 7-year-old has weakness rising from the feet over a week, absent reflexes everywhere and tingling toes. In the localizer, nerve and root both survive. Which conclusion is correct?
options: The localizer is wrong, because only one level can be affected
The muscle must be involved, because the weakness is symmetric
Both are correct, because Guillain-Barré syndrome is a polyradiculoneuropathy that damages roots and nerves
The anterior horn is the answer, because the reflexes are absent
quiz.explanation: Guillain-Barré syndrome is an immune attack on both the roots and the nerves, so a model that keeps both alive is describing the disease accurately and has not failed to choose. Insisting on a single level assumes one focal lesion, when the disease is a process spread along a whole system. Symmetric weakness on its own does not point to muscle, and a myopathy would not cause tingling. The anterior horn is purely motor, so although its disease also removes reflexes, it cannot explain the sensory symptoms.

quiz.question: In the localizer, a boy with a Gowers maneuver and proximal, purely motor weakness leaves horn cell and muscle tied. Which single bedside finding would break the tie most directly?
options: Weakness of hip flexion
Enlarged calves
Normal sensation in the feet
Fasciculations of the tongue or limbs
quiz.explanation: Fasciculations come from spontaneous firing of a diseased motor neuron or its axon, so they appear in anterior horn disease and never in primary muscle disease. Finding them breaks the tie toward the horn cell, and their absence leans toward muscle. Weakness of hip flexion is part of the proximal pattern that both addresses share. Enlarged calves suggest a dystrophy, but they are a softer sign. Normal sensation is expected at both addresses and so cannot separate them.

signOff: The resident examines three children with neuromuscular weakness and names the level of the motor unit before the EMG, agreeing with a faculty reader.

opener.parable: When a parent says their child has become weak, the problem can begin in four quite different places. It may lie in the nerve cell in the spinal cord, the nerve that carries its signal, the junction where nerve meets muscle, or the muscle itself. Each fails in its own characteristic way, and much of the examination is a matter of recognizing which.
opener.history: William Gowers (1845–1915), the Queen Square neurologist whose textbook was long called the neurologist's bible, gave his name to the way a child with weak hip muscles climbs up his own legs to stand.
